conbody.p: As it currently stands, joinder (the joining of defendants) in copyright litigation requires common questions of fact or law, and the defendant’s actions must be found to be arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences. Torrent sites segment large files into smaller pieces that can be downloaded in any order and pieced back together in a process known as “seeding,” meaning it can be downloaded by several users simultaneously, known as the “swarm.” In the past, MDJD litigation has often been allowed for instances of illegal downloading because all swarm participants are found to be involved in the same series of transactions or occurrences.

This allowance displays a fundamental misunderstanding of the way the internet operates. One illegal downloader can be acting in California while another is downloading the same file in Massachusetts. Sag specifies that a lower level of relatedness when allowing joinder is what plaintiffs, and specifically copyright trolls, have come to favor. Redefining the level of relatedness between defendants to mean those who have had direct contact with one another and acted together in participating in the same swarm when sharing files would decrease the frequency of MDJD litigation in instances of illegal downloading, preventing holders from using the practice for exploitative purposes.
